extracted.intended_audience: writers, poets, critics and cultivated readers interested in imagination, rhetorical craft, and social wit
extracted.subtask_description: Practical and critical guidance (18th‑century essay form) on how different writers — poets, fabulists, historians, natural philosophers — and conversationalists may shape language, imagery, and tone to gratify or affect the reader's imagination and social sensibilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poet's liberty: mend and perfect nature
rubrics_metrics.description: It is the part of a Poet to humour the Imagination in its own Notions, by mending and perfecting Nature where he describes a Reality, and by adding greater Beauties than are put together in Nature, where he describes a Fiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The poet may combine seasons, make flowers and trees coexist beyond natural limits, invent new species, order winds and rivers for delight — i.e., freely model Nature for the reader's imagination — but must not "reform her too much, and run into Absurdities, by endeavouring to excel." Examples given: combining spring and autumn blooms, creating groves of spices, cascading precipices of arbitrary height as pleasing devices; anti-pattern: excessive, absurd departures from plausibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fairy-way writing requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: The "Fairy Way of Writing" depends on the Poet's Fancy alone and requires a particular cast of fancy and an Imagination naturally fruitful and superstitious; the writer must be well versed in Legends, Fables, antiquated Romances, and popular Traditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because there is no real-world pattern, success needs a fertile, superstitious imagination plus knowledge of popular tales so the work harmonises with childhood prejudices. Make imaginary beings talk in a manner that is 'a little discoloured' — not like ordinary men — so their speech and sense seem proper to their condition. Shakespeare cited as exemplar. Avoid making spirits speak exactly like ordinary people.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of emblematical persons (allegory)
rubrics_metrics.description: Represent Passions, Appetites, Virtues or Vices under visible Shapes — making them Persons or Actors in a Poem (e.g., Hunger, Envy, Fame, Sin, Death).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allegorical/embodied abstractions can enliven the imagination when well managed; Spencer and the ancients provide strong examples. This device creates a new 'creation' within poetry and can be used to map intellectual ideas to material images.

rubrics_metrics.name: History: vivid, gradual unfolding of events
rubrics_metrics.description: Historians who please the imagination 'draw up his Armies and fight his Battels in proper Expressions,' set before the reader divisions, cabals and jealousies, and lead the reader step by step into the actions and events.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Present events in a way that unfolds by just degrees to keep the reader in pleasing suspense and to let expectations form; choose proper circumstances so the reader becomes a spectator and feels corresponding passions. Livy given as model. This is more an art of representation than a strict test of veracity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Natural philosophy: enlarge imagination through scale and marvels
rubrics_metrics.description: Writings in the new philosophy please imagination by revealing microscopic life, planetary systems, and the vast scale of the heavens, offering prospects that 'fill the Imagination with Astonishment.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use discoveries (telescopes, microscopes) and comparative scales (man → earth → planets → fixed stars → universe) to expand the imagination. Evoke both the very great and the very small to produce wonder; but be mindful of the imagination's limits (see separate criterion).

rubrics_metrics.name: Be aware of imagination's limits with extremes
rubrics_metrics.description: The imagination is confined and soon at a stand when it tries to take in things very great or very little; it cannot easily form distinct mental measures of extreme magnitudes or minuteness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize and work with the faculty's limits: while Reason may demonstrate infinite divisions, the Fancy loses sight; writers should therefore employ devices (gradual scaling, analogies) to help readers grasp extreme concepts rather than assuming raw description will suffice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose pleasing, accessible allusions
rubrics_metrics.description: The great art of a writer shows itself in the choice of pleasing Allusions, generally to be taken from the great or beautiful Works of Art or Nature; an Allusion's chief design is to illustrate and explain passages and should be borrowed from what is more known and common than the thing being explained.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer allusions from nature or widely known works rather than highly specialised sciences or narrow trades. Anti-patterns: scholars using obscure chemical or Cartesian references in ordinary discourse; men of business using low, trade-specific examples. Aim for allusions obvious to most readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use exact or agreeable metaphors
rubrics_metrics.description: A noble Metaphor, when placed to advantage, 'casts a kind of Glory' around a sentence; the likeness ought to be very exact, or very agreeable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select metaphors whose resemblance is either precise or emotionally pleasing. Misplaced or obscure comparisons lessen effect. A good metaphor illuminates and beautifies the passage; a bad one confuses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Descriptions: use words to powerfully affect the imagination
rubrics_metrics.description: The Power of Words over the Imagination explains why some readers prefer description and why one reader is more pleased with descriptions than another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Craft descriptive language to summon vivid images; choose particulars and arrange them to raise passion or astonishment. The writer's skill in description can create pleasure akin to seeing art or hearing music; tailor descriptions to likely reader sensibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make disagreeable subjects pleasing by apt description
rubrics_metrics.description: Anything that is unpleasant to behold may please the Imagination when well described; terror and grief can be pleasing when excited by apt descriptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When treating distressing or terrifying material, use apt, skillful description to convert disagreeableness into aesthetic pleasure — heightening the imagination and passion without gratuitous brutality. This relies on craftful representation rather than raw shock.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poets and fiction-writers have liberties but must use them judiciously
rubrics_metrics.description: Writers in poetry and fiction have advantages to please the Imagination because they may invent and take liberties not available to those describing real scenes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exploit the freedom to invent characters, scenes and faculties of soul (emblematical persons, new species, altered speech) to gratify imagination, but balance invention with plausibility and avoid plunging into absurdity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Raillery: aim to gain goodwill; avoid cutting wit
rubrics_metrics.description: In conversation, the first point to be aimed at is to gain the good Will of those with whom you converse; it is absurd to set up for being extremely sharp and biting to your familiars.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not use wit to shame interlocutors or force them into awkward explanations. A jest should not put someone to shame; the agreeable conversationalist makes others enjoy themselves rather than making them the butt of ridicule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Techniques for agreeable raillery
rubrics_metrics.description: To rally well, kindness must run through all you say; preserve the character of a friend; form ridicule upon circumstances the person is not unwilling to grant; sometimes insinuate shared fault so the person keeps countenance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Methods: (a) target a laudable excess (Callisthenes) so the person can accept the jest; (b) insinuate you share the fault (Minutius) to keep the person in countenance; (c) avoid malicious delight in another's discomfort (Acetus). Two practical rules: make the person either unaware they're rallied, or make them able to take it without offense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Satire should attack vice, not the person
rubrics_metrics.description: The most agreeable kind of raillery is when the satire is directed against Vice, with an air of contempt for the fault but no ill-will to the criminal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim the satirical sting at faults and vice while preserving humane regard for the individual. Congreve's Doris is offered as a model: a vicious character made laughable without maligning the person in a way that wounds the audience's sympathy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Courtship/social tactic: appear indifferent to win
rubrics_metrics.description: A practical social manoeuvre described: to gain the affection of a sensible woman, a man should be generally agreeable without addressing her in particular; studied unconcern or reserve may attract where open adoration does not.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by Strephon and Damon: the passionate, ostentatious lover tires and provokes scorn, whereas the civil, seemingly indifferent suitor gains favor by appearing disinterested. Watch for patterns of alternating behaviour and protect the loved one from subtle collusive strategies.
